statement: In people with alcohol or drug problems followed for between about a year and several decades, a large share no longer met the criteria for a problem at a later interview, many of them without treatment, but how many depends on who was counted (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, or people who had already recovered), on how a problem, recovery ('remission') and treatment were defined, and on the length of the time window. Of 451 men interviewed from a random sample of 470 US Army enlisted men who returned from Vietnam in September 1971 (interviews 8 to 12 months after return), 43% had used narcotics there (about a third of the men had tried heroin) and 20% reported having been dependent on narcotics there (21% by the study's own criteria for dependence), against 10% who had used narcotics and 0.7% who reported dependence (1% by the criteria) since their return; of 134 men from the study's two samples who were still dependent when they left Vietnam, 50% used narcotics again after return and 14% were dependent again (the two samples combined without weighting). The authors give a remission rate of 95% without saying which sample it describes; their figure, read approximately, shows that of the men first dependent in Vietnam, about 2% of 90 in the general sample and about 7% of 341 in a second sample (selected on a urine test at departure positive for narcotics, amphetamines or barbiturates) were dependent again. Remission there meant not being dependent again within about a year, many of the men counted as remitted still used narcotics, whether any had treatment is not reported, and the authors leave open whether the men's backgrounds or the change from Vietnam to home explains it (Robins et al., 1975). In a US national survey of adults interviewed in 2001–2002 and again about three years later (34,653 re-interviewed), 422 of the 1,172 people who met the criteria for alcohol dependence in the year before the first interview met them again in the year before the second (36%), so about 64% no longer met the full criteria (editors' calculation from unweighted counts), with persistence of 32.4% at ages 21–23 and 44.5% at ages 43–52; no longer meeting the full criteria can include people with one or two symptoms left, and treatment between the interviews is not reported (Vergés et al., 2012). In 21 cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, 15 of them recruited through treatment, followed for 3 to 50 years (mean 17), published 2000–2015 and mostly from the US, 54% (95% CI 42% to 66%) of the people followed to the end were in remission at the last follow-up, and 35% (25% to 46%) of everyone enrolled when deaths and people lost to follow-up were counted as not remitted; single cohorts ranged from about 20% to 96%, remission was higher in cohorts followed longer, and the 6 cohorts not in treatment at the start did not differ detectably from the treatment cohorts (62% against 51%, p 0.42). Treatment during follow-up was not analysed, the pooled figure mixes very different follow-up times and so describes no particular time point, and the review did not appraise its cohorts (Fleury et al., 2016). For alcohol problems, a review of 124 published estimates of recovery without treatment (27 studies, 1976–2018, 24 of them North American) found figures from 2.7% to 98.3%, largely because the studies counted different things: among people already recovered, the share never treated (78% in two Canadian population surveys); among people with an alcohol problem who stayed untreated, the share who recovered (in the US national survey of 2001–2002, 12.4% when recovery meant not drinking and 32.6% when moderate drinking also counted; in a Dutch survey, 78% of people with an alcohol use disorder who stayed untreated for three years were in remission at follow-up, against 40% of those whose disorder was moderate or severe; in one US cohort of people initially without treatment, 36.0% fell to 14.0% when recovery also had to hold 16 years later); and among everyone with an alcohol problem, the share who recovered without treatment, which gave the lowest figures (2.7% to 63.6% in the nine studies that allowed all three counts). Most estimates covered about one year, the review did not appraise the studies, and these figures are second-hand (Mellor et al., 2019). So a high share of never-treated people among those who recovered and a much lower share of everyone with a problem recovering without treatment in a year can both be right. No source read here measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol; for the Vietnam veterans, treatment was not reported. Certainty: very low. Status: replicated.
plain: Do people recover from drug or alcohol problems, even without treatment? Many do, but the numbers depend on how studies count. Of US soldiers in Vietnam, 20 in 100 said they had been dependent on narcotics there; in the year after coming home, about 1 in 100 had been. Whether they had treatment was not recorded. In a US survey, about 64 in 100 adults with alcohol dependence no longer had enough signs to count as dependent three years later, though some still had a few. In 21 long studies, mostly of people who had been in treatment, 35 to 54 in 100 were in recovery when last seen, on average 17 years later. For alcohol, studies of recovery without treatment give anything from about 3 to 98 in 100, mostly because they count different groups: among people who have recovered, many were never treated; among everyone with a drinking problem, fewer recover without treatment in a given year. Most of this is about alcohol or heroin.
population: US Army enlisted men returning from Vietnam in September 1971, interviewed 8 to 12 months later (451 in a random general sample; 898 in both samples) (Robins et al., 1975); US adults in a national household survey interviewed in 2001–2002 and 2004–2005 (34,653 re-interviewed; 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence at the first interview) (Vergés et al., 2012); 21 cohorts of people with alcohol, heroin or several-drug use disorders, 15 recruited through treatment, published 2000–2015 (Fleury et al., 2016); 27 studies of untreated remission from alcohol problems, 1976–2018, mostly North American (Mellor et al., 2019)
exposure: Having had an alcohol or drug problem (narcotic dependence in Vietnam, self-reported or by the study's own criteria; DSM-IV alcohol dependence; substance use disorders as each cohort diagnosed them; alcohol problems as each study defined them), with or without treatment as each study defined it
comparator: None (descriptive); the same people's earlier status; in the alcohol review, three different denominators (everyone with a problem, people who stayed untreated, people already recovered)
outcome: No longer meeting the criteria for the problem (remission) at a later interview or at the last follow-up, as each study defined it (not dependent again within about a year; not meeting full DSM-IV criteria in the year before an interview about three years later; at least six months without meeting criteria; abstinence or moderate drinking), and the share of it without treatment
magnitude: Robins et al. (1975), general sample N=451, before / in / since Vietnam: narcotic use 11% / 43% / 10%; dependence self-reported 0.2% / 20% / 0.7%, by the study's criteria 0.4% / 21% / 1%. Still dependent at departure (both samples, unweighted, n=134): 50% used narcotics after return, 14% dependent again. Men first dependent in Vietnam dependent again 8–10 months after return (Figure, approximate): about 2% (general sample, N=90) and about 7% (urine-positive sample, N=341). Stated remission rate 95% (no denominator). Vergés et al. (2012), NESARC 2001–2002 to 2004–2005: 422 of 1,172 with past-year alcohol dependence (36%) dependent again about three years later, about 64% not (editors' calculation, unweighted); persistence 32.4% (ages 21–23) and 44.5% (43–52). Fleury et al. (2016), 21 cohorts, follow-up 3–50 years: standard remission 54.4% (95% CI 42.1–66.2), cohorts 19.6–95.7%, I² 99.4%; conservative 35.0% (25.2–46.4), I² 99.5%; treatment at baseline 51.1% vs not 62.4% (p 0.421); longer follow-up, higher standard rate (B 0.046 per year, p 0.004). Mellor et al. (2019), alcohol, 124 estimates: 2.7% to 98.3%; nine studies with all three methods: all people with a problem 2.7–63.6%, untreated people 6.5–77.9%, remitted people 4.3–94.2% (unweighted medians 12.4, 38.9 and 43.9, not rates); 78% of remitted people untreated (two Canadian surveys); 12.4% vs 32.6% of untreated people remitted (abstinence vs abstinence or moderate drinking; NESARC); 78% vs 40% of people untreated for three years in remission (any vs moderate or severe disorder; Netherlands); 36.0% vs 14.0% (remission once vs also at 16 years; a US cohort).

risk_of_bias.note: The figures on recovery without treatment are second-hand from a review that did not appraise its 27 studies, many of whose estimates the reviewers calculated themselves (card sc_mellor_2019: narrative-review checklist, high); the meta-analysis did not appraise its cohorts and pools follow-ups of 3 to 50 years (card sc_fleury_2016: AMSTAR 2 critically low); the Vietnam study rests on self-report at one interview, study-specific criteria, a window of about a year and a 95% figure without a denominator (card sc_robins_1975: JBI moderate); in the national survey, offset includes people with residual symptoms and 20% were not re-interviewed (card sc_verges_2012). A claim seen through reviews is downgraded for risk of bias (METHODS 6.3).

inconsistency.note: Estimates range from 2.7% to 98.3%, but the review shows that the range follows mostly from the denominator and the definitions, and every source finds remission common on its own terms; not downgraded, because the statement ties each figure to its definition and sample.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: each figure is given with its population (young US enlisted men in 1971–1972; US adults with alcohol dependence in 2001–2005; mostly treatment-recruited cohorts; mostly North American alcohol studies), and the statement says that no source read measured recovery without treatment for drugs other than alcohol, except for the Vietnam veterans, whose treatment was not reported.

imprecision.note: Large samples behind the main figures; the Vietnam figures for dependence after return rest on small numbers (about 4 to 5 men dependent after return in the general sample) and approximate readings of a figure, stated as such.

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for descriptive survey figures; the alcohol review included every numeric estimate it found, whatever its size.

grade.reasoning: Descriptive claim: starts low and is rated as a description of the samples. Down one for risk of bias, because the part of the question about recovery without treatment rests on second-hand, unappraised estimates (and on a meta-analysis of unappraised, mostly treatment-recruited cohorts): very low. A lenient reading would rate the Vietnam and national-survey figures alone (primary data from a near-complete random sample and a weighted national survey) as low for the narrower statement that many people no longer meet the criteria within one to three years; the rating is set by the weakest necessary link. Not upgraded (descriptive). Status replicated: the direction holds in independent samples (Vietnam veterans; the US national survey; the cohorts pooled by Fleury et al.), but the US national survey appears in three sources (Vergés et al.; the lifetime cohort in Fleury et al.; Dawson et al. in Mellor et al.), which are not counted as independent of each other. Not used: the 95% remission rate as a figure (no stated denominator), Fleury et al.'s annual remission rates (inconsistent with its pooled proportions) and its 14 years of use before remission (not derivable from its table), and Mellor et al.'s medians as rates (card reporting issues).

statement: In people born from 1950 to 1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, both what was passed on from their biological parents and features of the adoptive home they grew up in were associated with a later register record of drug problems; the study estimated no heritability percentage. Of 18,115 adoptees followed in national registers to 2009 (a record meant a diagnosis of a drug use disorder or drug psychosis in hospital, outpatient, primary-care or death records; a conviction under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, convictions only for alcohol-related crimes or only for drug trafficking or possession not counting; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded; the study calls this 'drug abuse'), 4.5% had a record, against 2.9% of everyone in Sweden born in the same years. Adoptees whose biological parent had a record, though they were not raised by that parent, had one in 8.6% of cases against 4.2% when neither biological parent had (odds ratio 2.09, 95% CI 1.66 to 2.62), and in 11.9% when both had; records were also shared with biological siblings raised apart (full siblings, odds ratio 1.84, 1.28 to 2.64; half siblings, 1.41, 1.19 to 1.67). In the adoptive home, records were shared with adoptive siblings, who were not biologically related to the adoptee: 6.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees with a record had one, against 3.2% of the adoptive siblings of adoptees without (odds ratio 1.95, 1.43 to 2.65), and the adoptive mother's divorce and an adoptive parent's death were also associated with a record; adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with a record had one in 6.8% of cases against 4.5%, an imprecise estimate that included no difference (1.55, 0.86 to 2.80), with only 1.0% of adoptive parents affected. On the scale of absolute risk, an adverse adoptive home added more risk for adoptees whose biological relatives' records put them at higher risk, an interaction the paper does not report on the odds scale; at the lowest level of the biological-relative index the added risk could not be told apart from none (Kendler et al., 2012). An adoption study separates the family that passes on genes from the family that raises a child, but what passes from biological parents includes the pregnancy, care before placement (up to about 3 in 10 adoptees may have joined their adoptive family after age 5, by a census-based estimate) and how agencies matched children to homes (modest, by the authors' judgment), as well as genes. The authors report that children usually spent the time before placement in a nursery or foster home rather than with their biological parents, and that later placement did not go with a higher risk (odds ratio 0.96 per year before adjustment, 1.00 after); their argument against effects in the womb rests on 9.9% with an affected biological father against 8.2% with an affected mother, overlapping intervals without a test. As summarized, without figures, by a narrative review, twin studies find that genes and both shared and individual environment influence whether people start using tobacco, alcohol or cannabis, that genes matter more for regular use and dependence, and that the environment twins share is no longer detectable for regular use or dependence in adulthood though it is in adolescence (the adoptive-sibling association above, if it reflects the shared home, does not fit this summary well); single genetic variants have small effects that replicate poorly, scores combining many variants explained less than 1% of the variation in alcohol dependence, and the size of genetic influence has been reported to differ between environments (Prom-Wormley et al., 2017, second-hand). A heritability, where one is given, is a ratio: the share of the differences between people in one population, for a trait measured at a particular time or age, that goes with differences in their genes. It is not the share of any one person's risk, or of a trait, that comes from genes; a high heritability does not mean that genes fix the outcome or that the environment cannot change it (human height has a heritability of about 0.8, yet average height has risen over generations); and it says nothing about why groups differ or why levels change over time. Because it depends on how much the genes and the environments vary, it can change when environments change, with age and with how the trait is measured, and in theory a figure from one population does not predict another, though the heritabilities of similar traits are often similar across populations; for a diagnosis, the figure is much smaller on the observed yes-or-no scale than on an assumed underlying scale of liability when the condition is rare; and the classical twin design estimates only three variance components and overstates heritability when identical twins share more of their environment than non-identical twins do, or when genes and environments are correlated (Visscher et al., 2008, a conceptual review by geneticists that discusses no drug-use figure). Certainty: low. Status: single study.
plain: Do genes and the home you grow up in shape drug problems? In a large Swedish study of adopted children, both were linked to drug problems. Children whose birth parent had a drug problem in official records had one themselves about twice as often (about 9 in 100, against 4 in 100 when neither birth parent did), even though other parents raised them. Drug problems were also shared within adoptive families, between children not related by birth: when an adopted child had one, about 6 in 100 of their adoptive brothers and sisters did too, against 3 in 100 when the adopted child did not. Divorce or a parent's death in the adoptive family also went with more drug problems. The study did not work out a percentage due to genes, and what comes from birth parents also includes the pregnancy and the time before adoption. A percentage due to genes, where studies give one, describes differences between people in one place and time; it does not say how much of one person's risk comes from genes, it does not mean that the environment cannot change things, and it can change when living conditions change.
population: People born 1950–1993 and adopted in Sweden outside their biological family (adoptions by relatives or by a biological parent's partner excluded), with register information on both adoptive parents and at least one biological parent, who first lived with their adoptive parents by age 10 by a census-based estimate (18,115 adoptees; national registers to 2009); twin studies summarized without figures by a narrative review
exposure: A register record of drug problems in biological parents or in biological siblings not raised with the adoptee (what passes from biological relatives: genes, pregnancy, care before placement), and in adoptive siblings or parents, or disruption of the adoptive home (the rearing environment)
comparator: Adoptees whose biological, or adoptive, relatives had no such record
outcome: A register record of drug problems (the study's 'drug abuse': drug use disorder or drug psychosis diagnoses; convictions under two crime-register codes for crimes related to drug abuse, with alcohol-only, trafficking and possession convictions excluded; or long-term high-volume collection of prescribed sedatives, hypnotics or opioids; alcohol and tobacco excluded)
magnitude: Kendler et al. (2012): adoptees with a record 4.5% (95% CI 4.2–4.8; 820 people) vs 2.9% nationally for the same birth years. Biological parent with vs without a record 8.6% vs 4.2%, OR 2.09 (1.66–2.62); none, one or both biological parents 4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%; biological father 9.9% (7.2–12.1), mother 8.2% (6.3–10.5). Biological full siblings raised apart, record in 10.7% of the full siblings of adoptees with a record vs 6.1% of those of adoptees without, OR 1.84 (1.28–2.64); half siblings 7.4% vs 5.3%, OR 1.41 (1.19–1.67). Adoptive siblings of adoptees with vs without a record 6.2% vs 3.2%, OR 1.95 (1.43–2.65); adoptees raised by an adoptive parent with vs without a record 6.8% vs 4.5%, OR 1.55 (0.86–2.80). Interaction on the probability scale 0.0005 per decile × decile (0.0001–0.0008): each decile of the adoptive-home index added about 0.15 percentage points of risk at the lowest decile of the biological-relative index (the main effect with the interaction term, 0.0015, −0.0006 to 0.0036, an interval that includes no added risk) and about 0.6 at the highest (editors' calculation on the study card, recomputed with deciles coded 0 to 9). risk_of_bias.note: Not downgraded for the associations as worded (card sc_kendler_2012: ROBINS-E, some concerns): the national adoption design and a register outcome recorded independently of the study make the familial associations unlikely to be artefacts; the remaining concerns (pregnancy and care before placement, selective placement) bear on what the biological-parent association means, which the claim states, rather than on whether it exists. Families with criminal or psychiatric records may be more visible to police and services, which could inflate some associations.

inconsistency.note: One study; the biological and adoptive associations are consistent across kinds of relative.

indirectness.note: Rated as worded: Swedish adoptees born 1950–1993 with a biological parent in the registers (the paper does not say 'born in Sweden' or 'domestic adoptions') and a broad register construct, both stated; the gap to diagnosed use disorders, to other countries and to later cohorts is stated, not assumed away.

imprecision.note: Large cohort; the adoptive-parent estimate is imprecise (0.86 to 2.80), which the claim states; the sibling intervals may be too narrow if several siblings of one adoptee were counted as independent pairs (card reporting issue).

publication_bias.note: Not assessable for a single registry study.

grade.reasoning: Observational (a national register adoption cohort): starts low; not downgraded. Strict reading: counting the broad register outcome and the possibly too narrow sibling intervals as risk of bias would give very low. The gradient with the number of affected biological parents (4.2%, 8.2%, 11.9%) is not used as a dose–response upgrade: it concerns the biological side only, cannot separate genes from the pregnancy and care before placement, and the claim's weaker link, the adoptive home, shows no gradient (the adoptive-parent estimate is imprecise). No heritability percentage was estimated, the extreme-decile odds ratios in the paper overstate the contrast by one step and are not used (card reporting issue), and the gene-environment interaction holds on the probability scale only as reported, with the added risk at the lowest biological-relative level not distinguishable from none. The narrative review gives no figures for drug use disorders and is used for context only (second-hand). What a heritability does and does not mean now rests on Visscher et al. (2008), a conceptual narrative review by quantitative geneticists, used for definitions only: it discusses no drug-use figure, its numerical examples (height, IQ, livestock, schizophrenia and depression) are second-hand illustrations, two of its worked examples do not match its own formulas (card reporting issues), and it does not change the rating. Status single study.
